title: Examination of Desire and the Desirous

slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter six: the examination of desire and the desirous.

slides.heading: The one who wants
points: Someone who wants, and a wanting they have
The wanting comes and goes; the someone stays?
First, together, one or two?
slides.say: You want something: a cup of coffee, a person's approval, a new phone. There seems to be someone who wants, and a wanting that this someone has. The wanting comes and goes; the someone stays. The sixth chapter asks how the one who desires and the desire are related. Which comes first? Do they arise together? Are they one thing or two?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: From the furniture of the world to the afflictions
Beginning with desire, or passion
The question: together or apart?
slides.say: So far the chapters have looked at causes, motion, the senses, the aggregates and the elements, the furniture of the world. Chapter six turns to the afflictions, the states that drive suffering, beginning with desire or passion. It also gives the most careful working-out yet of the question together or apart, which the chapters ahead will use again and again.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Ten verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Which comes first?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter begins with order in time. Suppose the desirous person came first, existing before desire and free of it. Then desire could arise in dependence on him. But a person free of desire is not the desirous one. He is just someone. The name desirous needs the desire. Suppose instead that desire came first. Then where would it be? Desire is always someone's desire, for something. A desire floating free, belonging to no one, is never met. Order in time fails both ways, as the diagram shows.

slides.heading: Then together?
points: Born at the same moment is not related
One thing is not 'with' itself
Two separate things: what makes them together?
slides.say: The natural next move is to say they arise at the same moment. But two things that arise side by side, each complete, do not depend on each other. A cat and a dog born at the same moment in different towns are simultaneous, not related. Look more closely at together. For two things to be together, they must be either one thing or two. If they are one, they are not together: you do not keep yourself company. If they are two, really separate, each with its own nature, what makes them together? Their being separate gives no reason for it.

slides.heading: Oneness or separateness
slides.say: Verse six point five sharpens this. If togetherness came from oneness, it would not need a partner, since a single thing would be together all by itself. If togetherness came from separateness, it would not need a partner either, since anything separate from anything could be called together with it. Either way, together would hold without the companion it is supposed to be about. Togetherness cannot be built from oneness or from separateness, as long as each side is taken to have its own nature.

slides.heading: The circle
slides.say: Verses six to nine describe a trap the mind falls into. The opponent wants desire and the desirous one to be together. To be together, they must first be two separate things, so he assumes they are separate. But if they were already separate, each complete, there would be no need to say they were together. Then he turns the other way. Since they cannot be established as separate, he reaches for togetherness to explain them, and to make sense of togetherness he needs separateness again. Each answer is propped up by the other, like two cards leaning together. This loop is what happens whenever we try to relate two things we have first taken to be self-standing. The way out is not a better answer inside the loop. It is to drop the assumption that started it.

slides.heading: Neither together nor apart
points: Not a mysterious third relation
A negation that puts nothing in its place
Named in dependence on each other
slides.say: So desire is established neither together with the desirous one nor apart from him, and like desire, so with every phenomenon. The same lesson returns with fire and fuel, the agent and the action, and the self and its aggregates. Neither together nor apart is not a mysterious third relation. It refuses both answers without putting a new one in their place. What it leaves is the ordinary fact: someone is called desirous because of a desire, and a desire is called someone's because someone has it. That is all the relation there is, and it is enough.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: People still want things
Not a fixed owner, not an outside enemy
Desire changes when its conditions change
slides.say: People still want things, and the wanting still pulls. Buddhist practice takes desire very seriously, because it drives suffering. What the chapter removes is the picture of a fixed desirer who owns a desire as a thing, or of desire as a thing that seizes a person from outside. If there were a self-standing desirer, he could never be free of his desire. If desire were a self-standing thing, it could only be fought, like an enemy. Since neither is found, desire is seen as it is: an occurrence that arises in dependence on a body, a history, an object and an interpretation, and that changes when those change. Practice is not an attack on fixed defects but a way of arranging conditions.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: When a strong wanting arises, look at it
Where is the wanter, apart from the wanting?
It moves, and it can loosen
slides.say: Next time a strong wanting arises, look at it. Where is the wanter, apart from the wanting? Where is the wanting, apart from someone wanting something? The pull may still be there, vivid. But it is not a thing owned by a thing. It moves, and it can loosen.

slides.heading: In the books
points: The Logic of Dependency: conditions and openness
Substrateless World: Chapter 4
slides.say: The books do not discuss this chapter by name, but they take up its themes. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, shows anger arising in dependence on conditions, and practice changing the conditions rather than fighting a fixed defect. Chapter four of The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World explains why things defined together are not caught in a vicious circle, and how things meet as neither one nor two. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter seven, the examination of the conditioned.
